clinicalPearls: Defined by the triad of reduced or absent sweating (hypohidrosis), sparse hair (hypotrichosis), and missing or malformed teeth (hypodontia with conical teeth)
X-linked, so it predominantly affects boys, while carrier females may show milder or patchy features following lines of X-inactivation
Caused by mutations in EDA, which encodes ectodysplasin A, a signalling molecule needed for development of skin appendages
Impaired sweating causes recurrent unexplained fevers and heat intolerance, which can be dangerous in infancy and may present as fever of unknown origin
Characteristic facial features include frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge, and periorbital wrinkling or hyperpigmentation
Dryness of skin and mucosae predisposes to eczema, respiratory and ear infections, and reduced tear and saliva production
Management is supportive, focusing on temperature regulation, skin and mucosal care, and dental rehabilitation; carrier detection and genetic counselling are important
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the EDA gene, which encodes ectodysplasin A. This ligand signals through its receptor during embryonic development to direct formation of ectodermal appendages, including sweat and other exocrine glands, hair follicles, and tooth germs. Without functional signalling these structures fail to develop normally, producing absent or reduced eccrine sweat glands, sparse hair, and missing or malformed teeth. Loss of sweating removes a key route of heat dissipation, so affected individuals overheat readily and are prone to hyperthermia.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal forms of hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (EDAR, EDARADD)

additionalInvestigations: EDA genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and identify carriers
Assessment of sweating, such as sweat pore counts or pilocarpine-based sweat testing
Dental and orthopantomogram evaluation of tooth number and morphology
Skin biopsy showing reduced or absent eccrine glands where needed
Ophthalmological and salivary assessment for dryness
Temperature monitoring and evaluation of recurrent infections
redFlags: Hyperthermia or febrile seizures from impaired heat dissipation, especially in infants
Recurrent unexplained high fevers mistaken for infection
Failure to thrive with recurrent respiratory or ear infections
Heat-related collapse during hot weather or exertion
reference.prognosis: Intelligence and lifespan are usually normal with appropriate care; the main morbidity comes from heat intolerance and recurrent infections in early childhood and from the dental and cosmetic effects, which can be substantially improved with multidisciplinary and dental management.
pitfalls: Repeatedly investigating recurrent fevers for infection while overlooking impaired sweating
Missing subtle or patchy features in carrier females
Underestimating the risk of dangerous overheating in infancy
Neglecting early dental planning and psychological support
references: Standard clinical genetics texts on ectodermal dysplasias
management: Active thermoregulation with avoidance of overheating, cool environments, cooling garments and adequate hydration to prevent hyperthermia
Prompt recognition and management of unexplained fevers, which may reflect impaired sweating rather than infection
Regular emollients for dry skin and treatment of associated eczema
Early and staged dental rehabilitation with prostheses, and dental implants once growth allows, for hypodontia and conical teeth
Ocular and mucosal lubrication with artificial tears and saliva substitutes for reduced tear and saliva production
Treatment and monitoring of recurrent respiratory and ear infections
Multidisciplinary input from dermatology, paediatric dentistry, ENT and clinical genetics
Genetic counselling with EDA carrier testing for female relatives
